analysis.one_liner: Lets cities, towns, and co-ops offer their own broadband even when states try to block them.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Many states have laws, backed by large internet providers, that stop cities, counties, public-private partnerships, and co-ops from building their own high-speed internet networks. This bill would amend federal telecommunications law to say states cannot block those community-run providers, while requiring them to apply local rules fairly to private competitors [S2] [S3]. It was introduced in April 2023, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its communications subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Residents in states that restrict community broadband — especially rural and lower-income areas where big providers offer slow or expensive service — would gain another option when cities, co-ops, or public-private partnerships build networks. Local governments and electric or telephone co-ops would gain the legal right to serve their communities.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents underserved by big internet providers

how_it_helps.text: No state law could prohibit a public provider, public-private partnership, or cooperatively organized provider from offering advanced telecommunications capability (broadband) or services built on it [S3].

Public providers and government partners must apply their own ordinances and rules to competing private providers without favoring themselves, addressing the fairness objection to government-run networks [S2] [S3].
The bill does not exempt community providers from federal or state telecom rules that apply to everyone, so they would compete under the same regulatory obligations as private firms [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it passed, the cost would fall on incumbent cable and telephone companies that could face competition from city networks, co-ops, and partnerships in areas they currently serve with little rivalry. State governments with bans or restrictions would lose the authority to enforce them.

drawbacks.text: Critics argue government-run networks can fail financially and leave taxpayers on the hook for municipal broadband projects that don't attract enough subscribers; the bill's antidiscrimination and savings-clause provisions are meant to blunt, but do not eliminate, that concern [S2] [S3].

Private providers contend that government entities competing against them while also writing their local rules creates an uneven playing field; the bill responds by requiring non-discriminatory treatment of competitors, but private firms would still compete with entities that can tap public resources [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is real competition in places where one or two companies control broadband and prices are high or service is poor — community networks have worked in many places where private buildout stalled. The main cost falls on incumbent providers, who would lose the state-law shield that keeps potential rivals out. Risks of failed municipal projects exist, but the bill's fair-competition safeguards are designed to address exactly that objection.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and then passed to its communications subcommittee — and that is where it stayed until the two-year Congress ended in January 2025, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever scheduled [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Anna Eshoo introduced the Community Broadband Act on April 10, 2023, joined by eight original cosponsors including House Assistant Democratic Leader James Clyburn [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day it was introduced [S5].
On April 21, 2023, it was referred to the subcommittee on Communications and Technology, the last action the bill ever received [S5].
It picked up 22 cosponsors, all Democrats, but the Republican-controlled committee never took it up, and no version was introduced or advanced in the Senate during the 118th Congress [S4] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent broadband providers benefit most: the state laws that limit city, co-op, and public-private competition remain in force, and the markets they serve stay protected until a future Congress acts.

for.name: Anna Eshoo
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-CA), bill sponsor and senior member of the Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Community Broadband Act and recruited the original cosponsors; her committee seat gave her a path to push it, but the bill never reached a markup.

for.name: James Clyburn and eight original cosponsors
for.role: U.S. Representatives (D) — original cosponsors including the Assistant Democratic Leader
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; it later grew to 22 cosponsors, all Democrats.

against.name: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Her committee and its Communications and Technology subcommittee never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, keeping it off the House floor for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party in the 118th House of Representatives
against.what_they_did: Controlled committee calendars and floor scheduling; no member introduced a companion effort and the bill received no Republican cosponsors.

against.name: Incumbent cable and telephone broadband providers
against.role: Major telecom and cable companies and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: For years, industry groups have supported and lobbied for the state laws this bill would override, which bar or restrict city-run, co-op, and public-private broadband networks.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were Democrats and the bill was buried in a committee controlled by House Republicans, with no Republican support at any point [S4].

industries.note: Community networks, co-ops, and public-private partnerships would compete directly with incumbent providers in places where those providers now face little or no rivalry — often the same places with the slowest and most expensive service. The bill's failure keeps existing state-level restrictions on such competitors in place.

industries.industry: Municipal governments, public utilities, and telecommunications co-ops
industries.note: These entities are the bill's intended beneficiaries: it would give them the legal right to build and run broadband networks where state law currently blocks them. Because the bill died, that right never materialized.
